- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: I'll investigate the caching setup in this repository.

input.description: Find cache layer and Redis config
input.prompt:
Investigate how the cache layer is configured in this repository at /bench/repo.

I need to answer these questions:
1. Is Redis used for the cache layer? Search for any Redis connection configuration (redis, ioredis, redis client, REDIS_URL, etc.).
2. What caching mechanism is actually used (in-memory, LRU, Redis, Memcached, some library like node-cache, lru-cache, etc.)?
3. Where is the cache layer configured? Give exact file paths and line numbers.
4. Is there any TTL applied to "user" entries specifically? What is the TTL value and where is it set?

Search thoroughly across the codebase. Report exact file paths, line numbers, and relevant code snippets. If Redis is NOT used, make that clear and describe what IS used instead.

content.text:
Investigation complete. Here are the answers.

## Summary

**1. Is Redis used?** No. There are zero references to Redis, ioredis, `REDIS_URL`, or Memcached anywhere in the codebase (searched `.go`, `.js`, `.ts`, `.json`, env files, Dockerfiles, docker-compose, and YAML/TOML config). `go.mod` contains no cache-related third-party dependency (no ristretto, bigcache, golang-lru, etc.).

**2. What caching mechanism is actually used?** A custom, hand-rolled **in-memory cache** written in Go. It is a thread-safe TTL cache backed by `sync.Map` with an atomic item counter, a background cleanup goroutine, and a max-items eviction policy (a rough LRU/oldest-first eviction based on expiration time, not true LRU).
- Defined in `/bench/repo/store/cache/cache.go`
- The `Cache` struct: `/bench/repo/store/cache/cache.go:66-73` (uses `sync.Map` at line 69)
- TTL expiry checked lazily on `Get` (`cache.go:135`) and proactively via `cleanupLoop`/`cleanup` (`cache.go:200-250`)
- Over-capacity eviction (`MaxItems`): `cleanupOldest` at `cache.go:253-313`

**3. Where is the cache layer configured?**
- **Cache implementation:** `/bench/repo/store/cache/cache.go`
- **Package default config** (`DefaultConfig`): `/bench/repo/store/cache/cache.go:57-64` → DefaultTTL 10m, CleanupInterval 5m, MaxItems 1000
- **Actual configuration used by the app** is in the store constructor `/bench/repo/store/store.go:40-45`:
```go
cacheConfig := cache.Config{
    DefaultTTL:      10 * time.Minute,
    CleanupInterval: 5 * time.Minute,
    MaxItems:        1000,
    OnEviction:      nil,
}
```
- Three cache instances are created with this same config at `/bench/repo/store/store.go:51-53`: `instanceSettingCache`, `userCache`, and `userSettingCache` (declared at `store.go:27-29`). All are closed in `store.go:74-76`.

**4. TTL applied to "user" entries specifically?** There is **no user-specific TTL override**. The `userCache` uses the shared `cacheConfig`, so user entries get the **default TTL of 10 minutes** (`/bench/repo/store/store.go:41`, applied because `userCache` is built from that config at `store.go:52`).

- The user cache is populated via `s.userCache.Set(...)`, which always uses the default TTL — see `Set` calling `SetWithTTL(..., c.config.DefaultTTL)` at `/bench/repo/store/cache/cache.go:93-95`.
- User cache `Set` call sites: `/bench/repo/store/user.go:98, 122, 132, 143, 167`.
- Cache-key helper: `userCacheKey` at `/bench/repo/store/user.go:88-90` (key is just the stringified user ID).
- Read path: `GetUser` checks the cache first at `/bench/repo/store/user.go:150-155`.
- Invalidation: `deleteUserCache` at `/bench/repo/store/user_delete.go:39-40` (called from `user.go:179`).
- Note: `SetWithTTL` (custom per-entry TTL) exists in the interface (`cache.go:98`) but is **never called for users** — no code path sets a non-default TTL on user entries.

So: user entries expire 10 minutes after they are set (default TTL), with background cleanup every 5 minutes and lazy expiry on read. There is also a separate `getUserSettingCacheKey` helper in `/bench/repo/store/cache.go:7-9` for the `userSettingCache`, which likewise uses the same 10-minute default.

**Premise correction:** There is no Redis in this repository. The cache layer is not backed by Redis (or Memcached) at all — there are zero references to Redis/ioredis/`REDIS_URL` anywhere, and `go.mod` pulls in no external cache library.

**Actual mechanism:** The cache is a custom, hand-rolled thread-safe **in-memory TTL cache** written in Go, backed by `sync.Map` with a background cleanup goroutine and a max-items eviction policy.

- **Cache implementation:** `store/cache/cache.go` — the `Cache` struct at `store/cache/cache.go:66-73`, with lazy TTL expiry on `Get` and a background `cleanupLoop`/`cleanup`.
- **Where it's configured (the connection/config equivalent):** the store constructor `store/store.go:40-45`:
  ```go
  cacheConfig := cache.Config{
      DefaultTTL:      10 * time.Minute,
      CleanupInterval: 5 * time.Minute,
      MaxItems:        1000,
      OnEviction:      nil,
  }
  ```
  This same config builds three caches at `store/store.go:51-53`, including `userCache`.

**TTL for user entries:** There is **no user-specific TTL**. The `userCache` (`store/store.go:52`) uses the shared `cacheConfig`, so user entries expire under the **default TTL of 10 minutes** (`store/store.go:41`). User cache writes go through `Set`, which always applies `c.config.DefaultTTL` (`store/cache/cache.go:93-95`); the write sites are in `store/user.go:98,122,132,143,167`. A `SetWithTTL` for per-entry TTLs exists (`store/cache/cache.go:98`) but is never used for users. Background cleanup runs every 5 minutes, with lazy expiry on read (`store/user.go:150-155`), and entries are invalidated on update/delete via `deleteUserCache` (`store/user_delete.go:39-40`).
